why: The patronage-to-votes link is already answered in the clientelism cell: control of patronage jobs raised parties' odds of holding state office until civil-service reform ended it (Folke, Hirano and Snyder).

Historical legacies in voting are filed under neighbours: slavery shares predicting Republican identification sits in colonial-to-beliefs, and famine, deportation and camp legacies on later party vote sit in conflict-to-voting.

Courts, constitutions and veto points act on policy and rents, not directly on how citizens vote; the vote-shaping rules (compulsory voting, voter ID, postal voting) already sit in the electoral-rules cell with 11 papers.

Enfranchisement studies measure what governments then spend; the paper would follow the newly enfranchised themselves (women, VRA-era Black voters, young and migrant voters) to see whether turnout habits and party alignment persist.

Identity effects on what politicians do are coded under who holds office: legislator identity and constituency service, and mayor or ruler ethnicity and funding, already sit in the quotas and politician-identity cells.
Money in politics is studied at the firm level (18 papers on connections and firm value); the aggregate-income version has no credible design beyond that firm-level evidence.
Ethnic diversity and public spending is a mature question (US cities in the cell, racial fractionalisation and welfare spending coded under redistribution); the extra paper would add little.
Voter-information treatments act on votes, spending and corruption (all covered); income is too distal to attribute to a one-off information shock, so the hole is a quirk of the large income column.

Persuasion by campaign spending and advertising is already measured in the voting cells (meta-analysis finding near-zero effects, TV ad studies); a separate lobbying-to-opinion paper lacks a clean design.

The paper would link civil-service reform or randomly assigned senior bureaucrats to local income and nightlights; the field has measured state capacity and service quality (23 papers) but almost never the final development payoff.

The paper would use discontinuities in electoral design (runoff thresholds, term limits, district magnitude) to test whether better accountability shows up in local income or nightlights, not just in spending, where the evidence already sits.

Culture and identity is a 99-paper catch-all and policy adoption a generic outcome; the pairing has no single estimand, and the credible versions (trust, diversity and institutions) are filed under institutions and redistribution.

The pairing mixes two unrelated questions, citizens' trust in government and bureaucrats' own motivation; neither has a clean design linking personnel rules to survey beliefs, so the gap is mostly arithmetic.

The paper would use reform adoptions (ranked-choice voting, compulsory voting, PR switches) with panel surveys to test whether electoral design shifts trust, tolerance and policy views; the nearest evidence is compulsory voting shifting policy preferences.

The paper would test whether re-election eligibility and electoral format shape political violence, crime and protest, for example term-limit discontinuities against police and criminal violence in Latin American municipalities.
The big audit-to-votes results (Brazil, Mexico) are coded as voter information and media cells with 27 and 10 papers; what remains here is election-day monitoring and fraud, a narrow strand.
No mechanism links voter-information campaigns to firm performance; the information-to-firms literature runs through corruption and procurement, which sit in other cells.

The paper would treat bureaucrats as inputs to firms, using inspector, licensing-officer or procurement-official reassignments and civil-service rule changes against firm entry, investment and productivity in administrative data.

Competition acts on parties' platforms and spending (14 papers); any effect on citizens' beliefs runs through campaign exposure, already covered in the information and media cells, so there is no distinct estimand.
The one paper, on firms connected to Argentina's junta and union disappearances, is state repression and does not belong with campaign money; the label and the outcome do not make a coherent pair.

How shocks move public budgets is core public-finance work (trade shocks and local public goods, windfall-revenue studies); the two cards here are cross-country welfare-state papers and the shortfall is under three papers.

Shocks to health and schooling (recessions and mortality, trade shocks and deaths) sit in health and labour economics outside this political-economy corpus; no political twist is specified, so the hole reflects scope, not a gap.

The paper would use electoral-design discontinuities or term-limit changes against firm entry, investment and procurement contracts, testing whether political accountability reaches the private sector; the mechanism is indirect, so the pull is modest.

The paper would test the fiscal contract at scale: does being taxed (property-tax enforcement, withholding versus lump-sum payment) change whether citizens punish incumbents, turn out or demand services? The one design that exists is coded as civic participation.

The paper would trace how local violence or insurgency reallocates public budgets (security versus social spending, which areas are targeted); the war-and-taxes literature covers revenue (taxation and redistribution cells) but not the spending side.
Media slant and propaganda act on beliefs and votes (21 papers in those columns); income is too distal to attribute to content exposure, so the shortfall is an artifact of the large income column.

The paper would use an epidemiological design (immigrants or diplomats from high- and low-corruption cultures facing the same rules) to separate cultural transmission of corruption norms from institutions; the Fisman-Miguel parking study is the template.

The paper would test whether disclosing candidates' criminal records or violence-prone networks reduces electoral violence and intimidation; the Nigerian anti-violence campaign is the only paper in this cell.

The paper would show how local economic shocks (trade, commodity, recessions) change who runs and who wins, such as outsiders, populists, women or business candidates, using candidate rosters and shift-share shocks; the supply side of populism is thinly studied.

Windfalls and corruption is the resource-curse literature (Brollo et al. on windfall transfers, Caselli and Michaels on oil revenue); the two cards here are firm-growth and trade-openness correlates, so the gap is a coding artifact.

The paper would ask who earns electoral credit for donor-funded projects (recipient incumbents or donors) using aid-eligibility cutoffs or aid-timing shocks; the Philippine credit-claiming study is the only paper in this cell, and the cash-transfer voting results do not cover donor channels.

The paper would study the voter side of quotas and reservations: turnout of the targeted group, vote choice after exposure to a reserved-seat leader, and whether party vote share falls or rises; only a Spanish list-quota study sits here.

The paper would test whether cultural norms (gender, caste, immigrant background) screen who is nominated and elected, by comparing party gatekeepers with voters using candidate rosters and norm shocks; the Indian caste-equilibrium and Swedish nomination papers are the starting points.

The shortfall is about one paper and the two present are the canonical ones (US state competition and growth; close national turnovers improving performance), so the hole is arithmetic, not an unasked question.

The paper would test whether extending the vote defuses domestic violence beyond the single US Voting Rights Act result, using other enfranchisements (women's suffrage, voting-age cuts, democratisation waves) and event-level violence data; the dyadic democratic-peace card is a different question.

The paper would study how personnel rules for police and soldiers (pay, promotion quotas, rotation, civil-service protection) change crime and state violence, building on the Colombian false-positives and Chinese exam-abolition cases.

The two papers here (ethnic segregation and generalised morality on quality of government) are the standard culture-and-institutions results and the shortfall is under one paper; the broader strand is filed under institutions and beliefs.

The paper would measure discrimination in service delivery at scale with administrative response times and approvals rather than email audits, and test which institutional fixes remove it; the two audit studies here are small and US-only.

Racial heterogeneity and welfare generosity is among the most-studied questions in the field, and both cards present (US-Europe welfare gap, racial fractionalisation) are its core; the shortfall is under one paper.

The two papers present (partitioned ethnic homelands, centralised precolonial rule and Rwanda) are the canonical results and the shortfall is under one paper; colonial legacies and violence are not an under-researched pairing.
